title: It’s a play! What could it cost, 5 hours of your time? #theatre #play...
transcript: Would you see a 5 hour play about teenagers coming of age and playing D&D? Well, it immediately piqued my interest because I love a Marathon, and this new play Initiative kind of felt like binging a really well written miniseries. Taking place in the early 2000s, it follows seven or so teenagers from the beginning of high school through graduation, and all the highs and lows along the way, including forming a D&D group to find community and escape the stresses of an increasingly turbulent world outside. The big question I've had a few people ask me is, did it need to be five hours long? And that's not really the way that I was thinking about it, because after all, it's a coming of age story, right? Like, you could do a version of this in 90 minutes, or you could do a version of it over eight seasons of a TV show. The question for me is, what do you gain from the extended run time? And for me at least, there's something undeniably richer and more meaningful about getting to know these characters more deeply, going on a journey with them, and feeling the weight of the passage of time. I couldn't help but think of the hundreds of plays I've seen that are like 90 minutes in a living room, but they spend half the run time filling you in on everything that happened before. But here we get to see every relevant moment, play out for ourselves and carry that sense of history with us along the way. But obviously that effect wouldn't work if the writing and direction weren't as good as they are. If I were to describe the plot, it would probably sound a little bit like a series of cliches or like an after school special checklist. But the play rises above its familiar territory because the writing from Else Went and the direction from her wife, Emma Went feels so grounded and fleshed out, with so much room to breathe and characters that are meticulously crafted with love and care. So it feels like the events of the play are happening to real people that you know. And ultimately, the play fulfills the promise of its title with a found reflection on personal initiative, or lack thereof. What do these characters let themselves imagine for their own futures? and how does that fuel them to take action or fall into stagnation? Unfortunately, Initiative is closing on December 7th, just this weekend as I post this. But I could see this going on to become a quintessential coming of age play. With a small cast and simple set, I could also imagine it being produced all around the country if only people are willing to sit through five hours.
